title: Working with Text (Strings)
story: You're making a name tag for your desk. You want it BIG and BOLD so everyone can see it from across the room. Instead of shouting, you can make your program print your name in ALL CAPS — and even count how many letters it has!
why: Text is how programs talk to people. Almost every program you use — games, apps, websites — shows text on the screen. Knowing how to work with text is like learning to write instead of just saying numbers.
analogy: A string is like a bead necklace — each character is a bead, and `string.str_len()` counts the beads, while `string.str_upper()` paints them all the same bright color.
try_it: Print your name in ALL CAPS and count how many letters it has. Then try printing your full name (first + space + last) and count those letters too!
tips: Use `+` to glue strings together — don't forget to add spaces between words if you want them: `"Hello " + name`.
`string.str_len()` counts every character including spaces: `"a b"` has a length of 3.
`string.str_upper()` and `string.str_lower()` don't change the original string — they give you a new one.
You can store the result of any string function in a variable, just like you store numbers.
common_mistakes: Using `+` to glue a string and a number: `"Score: " + 5` won't work. Numbers and strings are different types.
Forgetting the space when gluing words: `first + last` becomes `"AlexChen"` instead of `"Alex Chen"`.
Trying to use `string.str_len()` on a number — it only works with strings, not numbers.
Thinking `string.str_upper(name)` changes `name` itself — it returns a new uppercase string, leaving the original alone.
